column30: Feature Description

Visualization and access of data produced by the VLF receiver sites. All data processing and visualization accomplished using vlfrx-tools software and standard Linux utilities. Processing and visualization functions don't require lots of memory and CPU resources.
column32:
The following data ingress products are accomplished with utilities in vlfrx-tools:

1. Ingress of compressed vorbis VLF streams (like an audio stream) to natural radio event detector, signal property measurements, and rotating buffer signal storage (20 or so days of low band width storage on rotating buffer).
2. Ingress (via rsync operation) of VLF transmitter data, both png file plots and amplitude/absolute phase data.
3. Ingress (via rsync operation) of raw data (flac compressed).
4. (Future) Ingress of sferic time of group arrival (TOGA) data (textual data on 2-minute interval for processing and entry into sferic database)
5. Lightning stroke locations on a map (possible postgresql database with postgis for mapping) calculated from sferic data.

column29: Automated within-band check with feedback to station operator
column30: An issue I've encountered, which can be subtle or blatant, is that of spectral clipping in the +/- 5Hz bandwidth (10 Hz sampling rate) used by the RX888 Mk2 stations (and perhaps others?). Accurate measurement of Doppler shift requires a spectrum without instrumental clipping of its high or low skirts. This can occur for a spectrum of modest width (~1 Hz) if the Doppler is substantial - as I see on multihop trans auroral oval WWVH to the UK for example. Or if the spectrum is wide, e.g. two hop sidescatter. Thinking ahead to the Antarctic deployments, checking that stations are using and reporting with adequate sampling rates is important for highest quality reduced data.
column32: With existing data I have resorted to clipping the Fourier components of the the other skirt to have a balanced spectrum for Doppler calculation where I've seen this behaviour.

column30: This probably falls under your words, " input on other aspects of the Personal Space Weather Station is also welcome". This feature is what I am currently working on in prep for AGU MacGyver. It is to use automated ray tracing (PyLap at an elevation increment of 0.005?) with a small suite of python scripts I've written / am writing to generate synthetic spectrograms. These spectrograms have the climatology of what rays can propagate from WWV to station X on frequency Y and what Doppler they have. I then know exactly what mode results in what Doppler. My concept is that the synthetic spectrogram would be overlaid (or underlaid) with the measured spectrogram to help elucidate the modes present, find missing modes, show weather vs climate etc etc.

RX888 Mk 2 receivers with WsprDaemon and ka6q-radio software are able to make measurements of the signal levels and, with new code, noise levels at the SMA input to the receiver. But between that SMA connector and the incoming signals there will be site-specific antennas, filters, preamps, splitters etc making the task of estimating the field strength of the incoming signals difficult.
Might there be a few reference sites where the equipment between the RX888 SMA and free space is a) as simple as possible and b) as well calibrated as possible such that these sites could provide field strength estimates? For example a few sites might be equipped with a Rohde and Schwarz HE010 antenna with its well-known calibration. At those sites such an installation could become a 'transfer standard' to calibrate co-located systems e.g. the DX Engineering 'monopole' active antenna.
